description: I am a second-year Electronic Engineering student passionate about utilizing structured logic and programming to solve complex problems in space exploration. For this challenge, I will be working independently to develop an interactive, data-driven health monitoring software using Python and modern frontend tools. My goal is to build a systematic, user-friendly UI that helps astronauts seamlessly track physiological indicators in isolated environments.
summary: AstroVita is a local-first astronaut health-monitoring prototype designed for missions where communication delays make continuous reliance on Earth-based systems impractical. Crew members can enter daily health indicators, receive a rule-based screening summary, explore how measurements relate to spaceflight hazards through an interactive five-zone anatomical map, and review a rolling seven-day trend chart. A repeatable mission system adds a behavioral-health engagement element by rewarding completed routines with a simulated Earth-communication bonus. AstroVita brings mission environment, physical readings, sleep, exercise, and self-reported mood into one crew-facing workflow. Its goal is to support awareness and timely communication with medical support—not to diagnose or replace mission protocols.
details:
AstroVita combines a React and Vite frontend with a local Python FastAPI backend. The browser sends a JSON health record to the backend’s /assess endpoint, where Pydantic validates the data and explicit screening rules produce an overall Green, Yellow, or Red status with hazard labels, warnings, and suggested next steps. Running the service locally avoids requiring a cloud round trip for the assessment workflow, which is useful when considering deep-space communication latency. The prototype does not provide a clinical decision system or guarantee operation without local power and software dependencies.

The crew enters a selected environment—Transit Spacecraft (0G), Lunar Base (1/6G), or Mars Rover (High Radiation)—along with a radiation-monitor alert, sleep duration, exercise minutes, blood pressure, SpO₂, heart rate, and mood. The backend adds environment-specific context and applies its current prototype rules, including alerts for selected mood states and heart-rate readings above 100 or below 50 bpm.

The interactive SVG spacesuit divides the body into five selectable zones: brain/helmet, lungs, heart, stomach/gut, and bones/muscles. Each zone explains a physiological function, links it to a human-spaceflight hazard, and displays relevant current inputs. A Recharts line chart displays systolic blood pressure, sleep, and SpO₂ in a seven-point FIFO window; after a successful health check, the oldest point is removed and the new submitted readings are added. A live routine countdown and repeatable mission-leveling loop encourage regular check-ins. Completing all three mission tasks triggers a level-up and a simulated 15-minute Earth video-call reward.
